## Loading Processed Kampala Rasters

```{r}
processed_files <- list.files(
  kampala_dir, 
  pattern = "_kampala\\.tif$", 
  full.names = TRUE
)

kampala_rasters <- list()

# Loop through and read each file
for (f in processed_files) {
  # Use the file name as the list key
  file_key <- basename(f)
  kampala_rasters[[file_key]] <- rast(f)
}

# The rasters are now accessible via the list, for example:
# kampala_rasters$ntl_2013_Q1_kampala.tif
```

```{r}
# Load the official administrative boundaries
roi_sf <- readRDS("./data/gadm/gadm41_UGA_1_pk.rds")
kampala_border <- roi_sf[roi_sf$NAME_1 == "Kampala"]
```

## Descriptive Statistics and NA Summary

```{r}
raster_summary <- data.frame(
  File_Name = character(),
  Total_Cells = numeric(),
  NA_Count = numeric(),
  NA_Percentage = numeric(),
  Min_Value = numeric(),
  Max_Value = numeric(),
  Mean_Value = numeric(),
  SD_Value = numeric(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Loop through the loaded rasters to calculate metrics
for (name in names(kampala_rasters)) {
  
  # Extract the current SpatRaster
  current_raster <- kampala_rasters[[name]]
  
  # Calculate total number of cells
  total_cells <- terra::ncell(current_raster)
  
  # Calculate exact number of NA cells
  na_count <- terra::global(is.na(current_raster), "sum")[1,1]
  
  # Calculate percentage of NA cells
  na_pct <- (na_count / total_cells) * 100
  
  # Calculate minimum value excluding NA
  min_val <- terra::global(current_raster, "min", na.rm = TRUE)[1,1]
  
  # Calculate maximum value excluding NA
  max_val <- terra::global(current_raster, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1,1]
  
  # Calculate mean value excluding NA
  mean_val <- terra::global(current_raster, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1,1]
  
  # Calculate standard deviation excluding NA
  sd_val <- terra::global(current_raster, "sd", na.rm = TRUE)[1,1]
  
  # Combine results into a temporary row
  row_data <- data.frame(
    File_Name = name,
    Total_Cells = total_cells,
    NA_Count = na_count,
    NA_Percentage = round(na_pct, 2),
    Min_Value = round(min_val, 4),
    Max_Value = round(max_val, 4),
    Mean_Value = round(mean_val, 4),
    SD_Value = round(sd_val, 4)
  )
  
  # Append to the main summary data frame
  raster_summary <- rbind(raster_summary, row_data)
}

raster_summary
```

# Spatial Fused Lasso, Kampala (Q3 2021)

Spatial fused lasso applied to Kampala nighttime lights – Q3 2021 (single quarter, 2D)

### Mathematical Formulation

The 2D Fused Lasso (also known as total variation denoising on a grid) estimates the regularized nighttime light intensity vector $\hat{\beta}$ by solving the following optimization problem:

$$ \hat{\beta} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \|y - \beta\|_2^2 + \lambda \|D\beta\|_1 \right\} $$

The objective function consists of two structural components:

-   **Data Fidelity Term (**$\frac{1}{2} \|y - \beta\|_2^2$): Measures the squared Euclidean distance between the observed log-transformed pixel intensities ($y$) and the estimated smooth signals ($\beta$). This component prevents the model from over-smoothing and deviating too far from the actual satellite observations.

-   **Sparsity Penalty (**$\|D\beta\|_1$): Applies an $L_1$ penalty (absolute sum) to the differences between spatially adjacent pixels.

-   **Tuning Parameter (**$\lambda \ge 0$): Controls the trade-off between keeping the original data structure ($\lambda = 0$) and forcing spatial homogeneity ($\lambda \to \infty$).

### Matrix Structure and Dimension Mapping

The `fusedlasso2d` function automatically constructs the structured penalization matrix $D$.

**Spatial Adjacency Penalty**

The penalty terms expand both horizontally and vertically across the Kampala grid coordinates:

$$ \|D\beta\|_1 = \sum_{\text{Horizontal Pairs}} |\beta_{\text{row}, \text{col}} - \beta_{\text{row}, \text{col}+1}| + \sum_{\text{Vertical Pairs}} |\beta_{\text{row}, \text{col}} - \beta_{\text{row}+1, \text{col}}| $$

**Parameter Alignment (Row-Major vs. Column-Major)**

-   **Data Input:** `terra::values()` extracts raster cells in **Row-Major** order (row by row, left to right).

-   **Solver Assumption:** `genlasso::fusedlasso2d()` natively expects data in **Column-Major** order (column by column).

-   **Correction Alignment:** Setting `dim1 = ncol_k` and `dim2 = nrow_k` correctly aligns the geometric boundaries of the 2D grid. This alignment ensures that horizontal and vertical neighbors in the mathematical graph match the true geographical neighbors in Kampala.

## 1. Extract matrix from raster

```{r}
r_kampala_square <- kampala_rasters$ntl_2021_Q3_kampala.tif

# Extract pixel values as a continuous numeric vector
v_kla_clean <- as.numeric(terra::values(r_kampala_square))

# Store the spatial grid dimensions
nrow_k <- terra::nrow(r_kampala_square)
ncol_k <- terra::ncol(r_kampala_square)
```

## 2. Fit 2D fused lasso

```{r}
# Fit the 2D Fused Lasso model
# fusedlasso2d builds the 2D difference operator internally
# dim1 maps to columns and dim2 maps to rows 
# because terra extracts values row-by-row (Row-Major order)
system.time(
  fit <- genlasso::fusedlasso2d(y = as.numeric(v_kla_clean), dim1 = nrow_k, dim2 = ncol_k)
)
length(fit$lambda); min(fit$lambda); max(fit$df)
```

**! ATTENTION:** The default `maxsteps = 2000` in `fusedlasso2d()` truncated the solution path before convergence ($n = 1710$; path stopped at $\text{df} = 123$, $\lambda_{\min} = 0.496$), covering only the large-$\lambda$ region and later producing a spurious monotonic BIC with no interior minimum.

**Fix:** `maxsteps = 8000` with `approx = TRUE` yields a complete path ($\text{df}_{\max} = 1709$, $\lambda_{\min} \approx 10^{-4}$, $\sim 125\text{s}$ runtime), revealing the expected U-shaped BIC and a well-defined optimal $\lambda$.

```{r}
system.time(
  fit <- genlasso::fusedlasso2d(y = as.numeric(v_kla_clean), dim1 = nrow_k, dim2 = ncol_k,
                                maxsteps = 8000, approx = TRUE)
)
length(fit$lambda); min(fit$lambda); max(fit$df)
```

The interpretation of the `genlasso` output path relies on the following core behaviors:

-   **Spatial Clustering (Piecewise Constant Patches):** The $L_1$ norm on the differences forces many adjacent pixel differences to become *exactly zero* ($\beta_i - \beta_j = 0 \implies \beta_i = \beta_j$). This process segments the Kampala metropolitan area into homogeneous economic or urban development blocks ("patches").

-   **Edge and Boundary Detection:** Pairs of adjacent pixels where $\beta_i - \beta_j \neq 0$ represent sharp spatial boundaries. In the context of nighttime lights, these boundaries isolate sudden transitions, such as moving from high-density commercial centers to unlit informal settlements or rural fringes.

-   **Solution Path Behavior (**$\lambda$ Mechanics):

    -   **Low** $\lambda$: High data fidelity. This setting retains localized noise, specific structural variations, and background satellite emissions.

    -   **Intermediate** $\lambda$: Optimal denoising. This configuration removes micro-level noise while preserving macro-regional clusters of economic activity and infrastructure development.

    -   **High** $\lambda$: Global smoothing. This parameter choice fuses all pixels together until Kampala collapses into a single uniform average light intensity value.

## 3. Choose lambda

### Option A(1) — Random K-fold Cross-Validation with Pixel-Wise Zero-Imputation

For each fold $k \in \{1, \dots, K\}$, the training vector $y^{(-k)}$ is modified by setting the test indices to zero. The model estimates the regularized coefficients $\hat{\beta}^{(-k)}(\lambda)$ along the safe lambda path grid:

$$\hat{\beta} \text{ extracted at } \lambda_j \implies \text{MSE}_k(\lambda_j) = \frac{1}{|T_k|} \sum_{i \in T_k} \left( y_i - \hat{\beta}^{(-k)}_i(\lambda_j) \right)^2$$

The optimal tuning parameter $\lambda_{\mathit{opt\_cv}}$ minimizes the average Cross-Validation Mean Squared Error ($\text{CV}_{\text{MSE}}$):

$$\text{CV}_{\text{MSE}}(\lambda_j) = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \text{MSE}_k(\lambda_j) \quad \implies \quad \lambda_{\mathit{opt\_cv}} = \arg\min_{\lambda_j} \text{CV}_{\text{MSE}}(\lambda_j)$$

Where:

-   $T_k$: The set of pixel indices assigned to the $k$-th test fold.

-   $|T_k|$: The total number of evaluation pixels within the active test fold.

-   $y_i$: The baseline observed log-transformed light intensity of pixel $i$.

**Methodological Limitations**

-   **Graph Disruption:** Random spatial sampling breaks the mathematical continuity of the 2D spatial adjacency matrix $D$.

-   **Imputation Proxy Bias:** Forcing $y_i = 0$ for test pixels introduces artificial sharp edges into the training phase, forcing the solver to smooth out artificial artificial contrasts.

-   **Interpretation:** The resulting curve provides a numerical profile of the cross-validation error across the tuning parameter grid. The selected $\lambda_{\mathit{opt\_cv}}$ marks the exact mathematical minimum where the model achieves the best balance between bias and variance. However, because random spatial sampling alters the underlying graph structure during the validation steps, this data-driven choice should always be verified visually to ensure that the resulting segments retain the true structural coherence of Kampala's urban boundaries.

``` r
set.seed(123)
n <- length(v_kla_clean)
K <- 5
folds <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = n))

# start timer
cv_time <- system.time({
  
  # 1. Pre-fit the folds
  fold_fits <- vector("list", K)
  max_min_lambda <- 0
  
  for (k in 1:K) {
    test_idx  <- which(folds == k)
    y_train   <- v_kla_clean
    
    # Set test values to 0 as an operational proxy for CV
    y_train[test_idx] <- 0  
    
    # Fit the model with corrected dimensions (dim1 = columns, dim2 = rows)
    fold_fits[[k]] <- fusedlasso2d(
      y    = as.numeric(y_train),
      dim1 = ncol_k,
      dim2 = nrow_k
    )
    
    # Track the highest minimum lambda across all folds to find a safe evaluation range
    max_min_lambda <- max(max_min_lambda, min(fold_fits[[k]]$lambda))
  }
  
  # 2. Define a safe grid of lambdas
  lambdas_safe <- fit$lambda[fit$lambda >= max_min_lambda]
  
  # 3. Compute CV Errors
  cv_errors_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = K, ncol = length(lambdas_safe))
  
  for (k in 1:K) {
    test_idx <- which(folds == k)
    
    for (j in seq_along(lambdas_safe)) {
      cv_errors_matrix[k, j] <- tryCatch({
        beta_j <- coef(fold_fits[[k]], lambda = lambdas_safe[j])$beta
        mean((v_kla_clean[test_idx] - beta_j[test_idx])^2)
      }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
    }
  }
  
  # 4. Identify Optimal Lambda
  # Computes the mean error for each lambda column, ignoring any NA
  cv_mse <- colMeans(cv_errors_matrix, na.rm = TRUE)
  lambda_opt_cv <- lambdas_safe[which.min(cv_mse)]
  
})  # end timer

cat("Optimal Lambda (CV):", lambda_opt_cv, "\n")

cat("CV computation time:\n")
print(cv_time)
```

``` r
# 5. Plot the CV Curve
plot(log(lambdas_safe), cv_mse, type = "l", col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "log(lambda)", ylab = "CV Mean Squared Error",
     main = "Cross-validation for 2D Fused Lasso")
abline(v = log(lambda_opt_cv), col = "red", lty = 2)

lambda_label <- paste0("Optimal log(lambda) = ", round(log(lambda_opt_cv), 3),
                       "\n(lambda = ", round(lambda_opt_cv, 3), ")")

text(x = log(lambda_opt_cv) + 0.1, 
     y = min(cv_mse) + 0.9 * (max(cv_mse) - min(cv_mse)), 
     labels = lambda_label, 
     col = "red", 
     adj = 0,         
     cex = 0.85)
```

### Option A(2) — Spatial K-fold Cross-Validation with Row-Block Mean-Imputation

For each fold $k \in \{1, \dots, K\}$, the study region is partitioned into spatial blocks defined by horizontal rows. The training vector $y^{(-k)}$ is constructed by replacing the held-out validation pixels with the mean intensity of the training sample:

$$y_i =\begin{cases}y_i & i \notin T_k \\\bar{y}_{-k} & i \in T_k\end{cases}$$

The 2D fused lasso model estimates the regularized coefficients $\hat{\beta}^{(-k)}(\lambda)$ along a safe solution path $\lambda_j \in \Lambda_{\text{safe}}$, where $\Lambda_{\text{safe}}$ is restricted to the lambda values generated by the model that are computationally stable across all folds ($\lambda_j \ge \max_k \{ \min(\Lambda_k) \}$).

The fold-specific prediction error for a given tuning parameter $\lambda_j$ is computed as:

$$\text{MSE}_k(\lambda_j) = \frac{1}{|T_k|} \sum_{i \in T_k} \left( y_i - \hat{\beta}^{(-k)}_i(\lambda_j) \right)^2$$

The optimal tuning parameter $\lambda_{\mathit{opt\_cv}}$ minimizes the average cross-validation error across all valid (non-convergent) folds:

$$\text{CV}_{\text{MSE}}(\lambda_j) = \frac{1}{K_j} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \text{MSE}_k(\lambda_j) \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{fold } k \text{ converged at } \lambda_j)$$

$$\Rightarrow \quad \lambda_{\mathit{opt\_cv}} = \arg\min_{\lambda_j} \text{CV}_{\text{MSE}}(\lambda_j)$$

Where:

-   $T_k$: Set of pixel indices assigned to the $k$-th spatial fold (horizontal block).

-   $|T_k|$: Number of pixels in the validation block.

-   $y_i$: Observed log-transformed nighttime light intensity at pixel $i$.

-   $\bar{y}_{-k}$: Mean intensity computed exclusively on the training folds (excluding $T_k$).

-   $K_j$: The number of folds that successfully converged for the penalty level $\lambda_j$.

**Methodological Limitations**

-   **Spatial dependence violation:** Although spatial blocks (horizontal bands) preserve spatial locality better than purely random sampling, residual spatial autocorrelation along the vertical and horizontal boundaries may still leak information between training and validation regions.

-   **Imputation approximation:** Held-out pixels are not truly removed from the optimization graph. Replacing them with the training mean $\bar{y}_{-k}$ is a pragmatic workaround required by the `fusedlasso2d` implementation, but it introduces a mild smoothing bias toward the global mean.

-   **Numerical convergence filtering:** The grid of evaluated hyperparameters must be truncated to $\Lambda_{\text{safe}}$. This heuristic ensures that $\lambda_{\mathit{opt\_cv}}$ is selected only from numerical regions where the fused lasso algorithm converges successfully across all folds, ignoring unstable paths.

-   **Boundary sensitivity:** The fused lasso objective function is highly sensitive to artificial boundaries introduced by the block partitioning, which may slightly bias the selected $\lambda$ toward smoother solutions.

``` r
set.seed(123)
n <- length(v_kla_clean)
K <- 5

# Create spatial folds using horizontal blocks
grid <- expand.grid(
  row = 1:nrow_k,
  col = 1:ncol_k
)

folds <- cut(
  grid$row,
  breaks = K,
  labels = FALSE
)

# start timer
cv_time <- system.time({
  
  # 1. Pre-fit the folds
  fold_fits <- vector("list", K)
  max_min_lambda <- 0
  
  for (k in 1:K) {
    test_idx <- which(folds == k)
    y_train <- v_kla_clean
    
    # Replace test pixels with training mean
    train_mean <- mean(v_kla_clean[-test_idx], na.rm = TRUE)
    y_train[test_idx] <- train_mean
    
    # Fit the model with corrected dimensions (dim1 = columns, dim2 = rows)
    fold_fits[[k]] <- fusedlasso2d(
      y = as.numeric(y_train),
      dim1 = ncol_k,
      dim2 = nrow_k
    )
    
    # Track the highest minimum lambda across all folds
    max_min_lambda <- max(max_min_lambda, min(fold_fits[[k]]$lambda))
  }
  
  # 2. Define a safe grid of lambdas
  lambdas_safe <- fit$lambda[fit$lambda >= max_min_lambda]
  
  # 3. Compute CV Errors
  cv_errors <- numeric(length(lambdas_safe))
  cv_counts <- numeric(length(lambdas_safe))
  
  for (k in 1:K) {
    test_idx <- which(folds == k)
    
    for (j in seq_along(lambdas_safe)) {
      res <- tryCatch({
        beta_j <- coef(fold_fits[[k]], lambda = lambdas_safe[j])$beta
        mean((v_kla_clean[test_idx] - beta_j[test_idx])^2, na.rm = TRUE)
      }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
      
      if (!is.na(res)) {
        cv_errors[j] <- cv_errors[j] + res
        cv_counts[j] <- cv_counts[j] + 1
      }
    }
  }
  
  # 4. Identify optimal lambda
  cv_mse <- cv_errors / cv_counts
  lambda_opt_cv <- lambdas_safe[which.min(cv_mse)]
  
})  # end timer

cat("Optimal Lambda (Spatial CV):", lambda_opt_cv, "\n")

cat("CV computation time:\n")
print(cv_time)
```

``` r
# 5. Plot the CV Curve
plot(log(lambdas_safe), cv_mse, type = "l", col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "log(lambda)", ylab = "CV Mean Squared Error",
     main = "Cross-validation for 2D Fused Lasso")
abline(v = log(lambda_opt_cv), col = "red", lty = 2)

lambda_label <- paste0("Optimal log(lambda) = ", round(log(lambda_opt_cv), 3),
                       "\n(lambda = ", round(lambda_opt_cv, 3), ")")

text(x = log(lambda_opt_cv) + 0.1, 
     y = min(cv_mse) + 0.9 * (max(cv_mse) - min(cv_mse)), 
     labels = lambda_label, 
     col = "red", 
     adj = 0,         
     cex = 0.85)
```

### Option B(1) — Lambda Selection via Schwarz Information Criterion (BIC)

The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) balances the goodness of fit against the structural complexity of the spatial graph. The canonical objective criteria is defined as:

$$\text{BIC}(\lambda) = n \log\left(\frac{\text{RSS}(\lambda)}{n}\right) + \text{df}(\lambda) \log(n)$$

Where the specific metric functions expand as:

-   **Residual Sum of Squares** ($\text{RSS}(\lambda)$): $\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{\beta}_i(\lambda))^2$, evaluating the empirical error variance.

-   **Degrees of Freedom** ($\text{df}(\lambda)$): In a 2D Fused Lasso setup, the effective degrees of freedom quantify the number of independent parameters retained after accounting for the fusion constraints imposed by the penalty term. In spatial applications, this quantity is related to the number of connected constant regions generated on the raster grid at a given penalty level $\lambda$ and is used as a measure of model complexity.

**Why BIC is Superior to K-fold CV for Spatial Rasters**

-   **Preservation of Topology:** BIC operates globally on the original, uncompromised raster grid. It eliminates the need to randomly mask or zero-out pixels, avoiding the creation of artificial spatial boundaries.

-   **Pathwise Degrees of Freedom:** The `genlasso` package computes the generalized lasso solution path for a sequence of regularization parameters. For each solution along the path, an effective degrees of freedom measure is provided and incorporated into the BIC-type criterion as a penalty for model complexity. In the fused lasso setting, increasing values of degrees of freedom indicate solutions with a larger number of independent spatial regions and reduced fusion between neighboring pixels. Therefore, the BIC criterion penalizes solutions that achieve a better data fit at the cost of excessive spatial fragmentation.

-   **Computational Efficiency:** Unlike Cross-Validation, which requires re-running the heavy 2D solver $K$ separate times, BIC is evaluated post-hoc on the full solution path object in a fraction of a second.

```{r}
# 1. Data Preparation
y_vec <- as.numeric(v_kla_clean)
n <- length(y_vec)

# 2. Extract Coefficient Matrix
beta_mat <- as.matrix(fit$beta) 

# 3. Calculate Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)
rss <- colSums((beta_mat - y_vec)^2)

# 4. Degrees of Freedom
df_vec <- fit$df

# 5. Compute BIC Score (Canonical Formula)
# n * log(RSS / n) + df * log(n)
bic_values <- n * log(rss / n) + df_vec * log(n)

# 6. Identify Optimal Lambda
best_idx <- which.min(bic_values)
lambda_opt_bic <- fit$lambda[best_idx]

cat("Optimal Lambda selected (BIC):", lambda_opt_bic, "\n")
```

```{r}
# 7. Visualization of the selection process
plot(log(fit$lambda), bic_values, type = "l", col = "darkblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "log(lambda)", ylab = "BIC Score",
     main = "Optimal Lambda Selection via BIC")
abline(v = log(lambda_opt_bic), col = "red", lty = 2)

lambda_label_bic <- paste0("Optimal log(lambda) = ", round(log(lambda_opt_bic), 3),
                           "\n(lambda = ", round(lambda_opt_bic, 3), ")")

text(x = log(lambda_opt_bic) + 0.1, 
     y = min(bic_values) + 0.9 * (max(bic_values) - min(bic_values)), 
     labels = lambda_label_bic, 
     col = "red", 
     adj = 0,         
     cex = 0.85)
```

### Option B(2) — Lambda Selection via Pathwise Scaled BIC

The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) is a widely used model selection principle that balances goodness of fit and model complexity in penalized regression frameworks. For sparse estimators such as LASSO and the 2D Fused Lasso, model selection is commonly performed along the regularization path by evaluating the trade-off between residual error and effective degrees of freedom.

To obtain a variance-normalized selection criterion suitable for high-resolution spatial settings, a BIC-type formulation is adopted. The criterion is evaluated at each value of the regularization parameter $\lambda$ along the solution path:

$$\text{BIC}(\lambda) = \frac{\text{RSS}(\lambda)}{\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{Neumann}}(k^*)} + \text{df}(\lambda) \log(n)$$

Unlike the classical likelihood-based BIC formulation, which relies on the logarithm of the residual variance, this criterion uses a variance-scaled residual term. This formulation is intended as a BIC-inspired selection score adapted to the spatial fused lasso setting.

Where the specific metric functions expand as:

-   **Residual Sum of Squares** ($\text{RSS}(\lambda)$): $\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{\beta}_i(\lambda))^2$, measuring the data fidelity term associated with a given penalty level $\lambda$.

-   **Data-Driven Error Variance Estimate** ($\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{Neumann}}(k^*)$): A data-driven estimate of the background noise variance computed directly from the observed raster before fitting the fused lasso path.

-   **Degrees of Freedom** ($\text{df}(\lambda)$): In a 2D Fused Lasso setup, the degrees of freedom are given by the number of connected constant spatial blocks (a standard approximation of the effective degrees of freedom in fused lasso models), corresponding to the number of separated, constant spatial regions (connected components) generated on the grid at a given penalty level $\lambda$.

**Advantages of the Variance-Scaled Criterion for Spatial Raster Data**

-   **Resolution of Path-Dependent Circularity**: The variance estimate $\hat{\sigma}^2$$ is computed directly from the observed raster before evaluating the fused lasso solution path. Therefore, the estimated noise scale remains independent of the regularization parameter $\lambda$, avoiding potential interactions between the variance estimate and the model complexity along the solution path.

-   **Asymptotic Stability against** $\text{RSS} \to 0$: In 2D Fused Lasso, when $\lambda$ approaches zero, the model becomes highly flexible and closely fits the pixel grid. In the classical likelihood-based BIC formulation, the term $n \log(\text{RSS}/n)$ can become numerically unstable in highly flexible regions of the solution path, where the residual sum of squares becomes very small relative to $n$, and may dominate the degrees of freedom penalty, potentially leading to overly complex solutions along the path. Conditioning the criterion on a fixed $\hat{\sigma}^2$ replaces the logarithmic likelihood term with a variance-scaled residual expression, resulting in a more stable and well-behaved selection curve.

-   **Use of the Full Spatial Structure:** The criterion is evaluated on the complete raster grid without requiring additional spatial partitioning strategies. This avoids introducing artificial boundaries that may affect the spatial continuity of the fused lasso solution.

-   **Pathwise Degrees of Freedom:** The `genlasso` package computes the generalized lasso solution path for a sequence of regularization parameters. For each solution along the path, an effective degrees of freedom measure is provided and incorporated into the BIC-type criterion as a penalty for model complexity. In the fused lasso setting, increasing values of degrees of freedom indicate solutions with a larger number of independent spatial regions and reduced fusion between neighboring pixels. Therefore, the BIC criterion penalizes solutions that achieve a better data fit at the cost of excessive spatial fragmentation.

-   **Computational Efficiency:** Unlike Cross-Validation, which requires re-running the heavy 2D solver $K$ separate times, BIC is evaluated post-hoc on the full solution path object in a fraction of a second, requiring a single computation of the solution path.

### Spatial Decorrelation and Data-Driven Stride Selection

High-resolution satellite imagery commonly exhibits spatial dependence at short distances due to both sensor-related effects, such as the optical Point Spread Function (PSF), and intrinsic spatial continuity of the observed landscape. As a consequence, a first-difference variance estimator based exclusively on adjacent pixels may capture a mixture of stochastic noise and local signal variation rather than the noise component alone. When the local spatial signal dominates the random component, the resulting variance estimate can be biased downward, affecting the scale of the information criterion.

High-resolution satellite imagery commonly exhibits short-range spatial dependence due to both sensor characteristics and spatial continuity of the observed surface. Therefore, adjacent-pixel differences may contain both stochastic noise and structured spatial variation, leading to a biased estimate of the noise variance when first-order differences are used directly.

To isolate the stochastic noise component objectively, the spatial decorrelation distance is evaluated directly from the empirical dataset prior to entering the path selection. Rather than computing a global Autocorrelation Function (ACF), which would confound micro-scale pixel dependencies with macro-urban structural layout, the ACF is evaluated locally row-by-row on the extracted raster matrix $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{R \times C}$ up to a maximum lag of 10, and then averaged across the entire grid:

$$\bar{\rho}(h) = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{i=1}^{R} \rho_i(h)$$

Where $\rho_i(h)$ represents the empirical autocorrelation coefficient of row $i$ at spatial lag $h$, and $R$ is the total number of rows. The optimal spatial stride ($k^*$) is defined as the earliest lag at which the average horizontal autocorrelation falls below a conservative significance threshold of $0.20$:

$$k^* = \min \left\{ h \in \mathbb{N}^+ : \bar{\rho}(h) < 0.20 \right\}$$

This $0.20$ threshold represents the critical boundary where approximately $80\%$ of the localized neighbor-to-neighbor shared variance is dissipated. If the structural spatial correlation is exceptionally persistent and does not cross this threshold within the evaluated window, a safety fallback value of $k^* = 3$ is automatically applied to guarantee execution.

```{r}
# 1. Extract the original data matrix from the raster object
mat <- terra::as.matrix(r_kampala_square, wide = TRUE)

# 2. Configure Autocorrelation Function (ACF) parameters
max_lag <- 10
acf_rows <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(mat), ncol = max_lag + 1)

# 3. Compute row-by-row ACF to isolate local pixel behavior
for(i in 1:nrow(mat)) {
  acf_rows[i, ] <- acf(mat[i, ], lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)$acf
}
acf_mean_horizontal <- colMeans(acf_rows)

# 4. Define the critical threshold for local decorrelation
decorrelation_threshold <- 0.20

# 5. Extract the optimal lag dropping below the threshold (excluding lag 0)
optimal_step <- which(acf_mean_horizontal[-1] < decorrelation_threshold)[1]

# Automatic fallback if no lag drops below the specified threshold
if (is.na(optimal_step)) optimal_step <- 3

print(optimal_step)
```

### The Lag-K Spatial Neumann Estimator Formula

Once the data-driven stride ($k^*$) is established, it parameterizes a modified first-difference estimator applied along both the horizontal and vertical topologies of the matrix grid:

$$\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{Neumann}}(k^*) = \frac{1}{4} \left[ \text{mean}\left( (\mathbf{Y}_{i, j + k^*} - \mathbf{Y}_{i, j})^2 \right) + \text{mean}\left( (\mathbf{Y}_{i + k^*, j} - \mathbf{Y}_{i, j})^2 \right) \right]$$

The operational mechanism of this estimator relies on three structural components:

-   Spatial Differences at Distance $k^*$: The terms $(\mathbf{Y}_{i, j + k^*} - \mathbf{Y}_{i, j})$ and $(\mathbf{Y}_{i + k^*, j} - \mathbf{Y}_{i, j})$ compute the forward differences across rows and columns using the optimal stride. By bypassing the immediate neighbors and spanning the exact distance $k^*$, the subtraction neutralizes the underlying geographic signal (macro-urban trends) while ensuring that the pixel values being compared are sufficiently decorrelated from the instrument's sensor blurring.

-   Average Squared Variations: Squaring the differences eliminates directional signs, preventing positive and negative spatial fluctuations from canceling each other out. Taking the global mean of these squared terms across all valid coordinate sub-matrices yields a robust, non-parametric measure of the overall residual volatility within the scene.

-   Unbiased Scaling Factor: By definition, the variance of the difference between two independent and identically distributed random variables is the sum of their individual variances ($\text{Var}(A - B) = \text{Var}(A) + \text{Var}(B) = 2\sigma^2$). Because this variance doubling occurs independently across both the row and column directions, evaluating differences along a 2D spatial grid compounds the scaling factor. Introducing the coefficient $\frac{1}{4}$ corrects this dual duplication, returning an unbiased, anchored estimation of the pure background stochastic noise ($\hat{\sigma}^2$).

```{r}
# 1. Data Preparation
y_vec <- as.numeric(v_kla_clean)
n <- length(y_vec)
beta_mat <- as.matrix(fit$beta) 

# 2. Calculate Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)
rss <- colSums((beta_mat - y_vec)^2)
df_vec <- fit$df

# 3. Reshape Original Data Vector to 2D Spatial Grid
# Reconstruct the matrix using only the observed pixel values row-by-row
mat <- matrix(y_vec, nrow = nrow_k, ncol = ncol_k, byrow = TRUE)

# 4. Estimate Error Variance (Sigma^2) via Spatial Lag-K Neumann Estimator
# Compute horizontal and vertical spatial differences using the pre-calculated optimal step
diff_h <- mat[, -(1:optimal_step), drop = FALSE] - mat[, -((ncol(mat) - (optimal_step - 1)):ncol(mat)), drop = FALSE]
diff_v <- mat[-(1:optimal_step), , drop = FALSE] - mat[-((nrow(mat) - (optimal_step - 1)):nrow(mat)), , drop = FALSE]

# Final Lag-K Neumann variance estimate (mean of squared differences divided by 4)
sig2_est <- (mean(diff_h^2) + mean(diff_v^2)) / 4

# 5. Compute Sparsity-Stable BIC Score
bic_values_psbic <- (rss / sig2_est) + (df_vec * log(n))

# 6. Identify Optimal Lambda
best_idx_psbic <- which.min(bic_values_psbic)
lambda_opt_bic_psbic <- fit$lambda[best_idx_psbic]

cat("Optimal Lambda selected (Lag-K Stride Neumann Var):", lambda_opt_bic_psbic, "\n")
```

```{r}
# 7. Visualization of the selection process
df_plot <- data.frame(
  log_lambda = log(fit$lambda),
  bic = bic_values_psbic
)

x_opt <- log(lambda_opt_bic_psbic)
lambda_label_psbic <- bquote(
  atop(
    "Optimal " * log(lambda) == .(round(x_opt, 3)),
    "(" * lambda == .(round(lambda_opt_bic_psbic, 3)) * ")"
  )
)

quarter_label <- gsub("_", " ", sub(".*_(\\d{4}_Q\\d)_.*", "\\1", raster_source))

y_pos <- min(df_plot$bic) + 0.9 * (max(df_plot$bic) - min(df_plot$bic))

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = log_lambda, y = bic)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkblue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x_opt, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text",

  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(floor(min(df_plot$log_lambda)), ceiling(max(df_plot$log_lambda)), by = 0.5)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Optimal Lambda Selection via Pathwise Scaled BIC — ", quarter_label),
    subtitle = paste0("Variance Estimated via Data-Driven Spatial Lag-", optimal_step, " Neumann Estimator"),
    x = expression(log(lambda)),
    y = "Pathwise Scaled BIC Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, size = 14, margin = margin(b = 4)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray40", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
```

### Alternative Approach: Second-Order Differences for Local Trend Removal

While the Lag-K stride approach effectively removes local sensor blurring by expanding the step size, persistent macro-urban trends can sometimes remain if the optimal lag is small. An alternative formulation uses second-order discrete differences (at a fixed lag of 1) to eliminate linear local trends entirely before estimating the background noise variance.

The second-order difference operator along the horizontal and vertical grid axes is defined as:

$$\Delta^{(2)} \mathbf{Y}_{i,j} = \mathbf{Y}_{i, j+1} - 2\mathbf{Y}_{i, j} + \mathbf{Y}_{i, j-1}$$

The variance scale factor for this discrete operator is derived from the sum of the squared coefficients ($\sum c_k^2 = 1^2 + (-2)^2 + 1^2 = 6$). Evaluating this independently across both rows and columns yields the following variance estimator:

$$\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{Diff2}} = \frac{1}{6} \left[ \text{mean}\left( (\Delta^{(2)}_h \mathbf{Y})^2 \right) + \text{mean}\left( (\Delta^{(2)}_v \mathbf{Y})^2 \right) \right]$$

```{r}
# 1. Reshape Original Data Vector to 2D Spatial Grid
mat_grid <- matrix(y_vec, nrow = nrow_k, ncol = ncol_k, byrow = TRUE)

# 2. Compute Second-Order Differences (lag = 1)
diff2_h <- mat_grid[, 3:ncol(mat_grid)] - 2 * mat_grid[, 2:(ncol(mat_grid)-1)] + mat_grid[, 1:(ncol(mat_grid)-2)]
diff2_v <- mat_grid[3:nrow(mat_grid), ] - 2 * mat_grid[2:(nrow(mat_grid)-1), ] + mat_grid[1:(nrow(mat_grid)-2), ]

# 3. Estimate Error Variance via Second-Order Differences (scaled by 6 for rows and columns)
sig2_est_diff2 <- (mean(diff2_h^2) / 6) + (mean(diff2_v^2) / 6)

# 4. Compute Sparsity-Stable BIC Score with Second-Order Variance
bic_values_diff2 <- (rss / sig2_est_diff2) + (df_vec * log(n))

# 5. Identify Optimal Lambda
best_idx_diff2 <- which.min(bic_values_diff2)
lambda_opt_diff2 <- fit$lambda[best_idx_diff2]

cat("Optimal Lambda selected (Second-Order Differences):", lambda_opt_diff2, "\n")
```

## 4. Extract smoothed coefficients

Because the input vector $y \in \mathbb{R}^N$ was completely cleaned of missing values during the early preprocessing phase, the optimization domain directly covers the full coordinate space of the spatial grid. The extraction of the estimated parameter vector $\beta^*(\lambda)$ simplifies to a direct identity assignment:

$$\beta^*_i = \hat{\beta}_i(\lambda_{\text{selected}}) \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$$

Where $N$ represents both the complete length of `v_kla_clean` and the exact total pixel count within the structural dimensions of the Kampala raster.

**Methodological Implications**

-   **Computational Integrity:** The absence of spatial masking means that every single element inside `beta_smooth` maps sequentially to a specific row and column in the geographic grid without index displacement.

-   **Direct Raster Coercion:** This streamlined setup allows the vector to be reshaped into a matrix or converted directly into a spatial object (`terra::rast`) in the next step, ensuring that the spatial orientation of the nighttime light clusters remains mathematically uncorrupted.

```{r}
# Define which optimal lambda to use for the final map extraction
# Change to lambda_opt (BIC) or use a manual value from the visual elbow (e.g., 2.5)
selected_lambda <- lambda_opt_diff2

# 1. Extract the smoothed beta coefficients from the solution path
# Since there are no NAs, beta_smooth maps 1:1 to the clean spatial grid length
beta_smooth <- coef(fit, lambda = selected_lambda)$beta
```

## 5. Rebuild raster

The assignment operation overwrites the internal data matrix containing the empirical radiance values while leaving the spatial metadata fully intact. Mathematically, the vector transformation maps the continuous parameter space back to a two-dimensional coordinate framework defined by the spatial bounding box:

$$\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathit{nrow\_k} \times \mathit{ncol\_k}}$$

Where:

-   $\mathit{nrow\_k}$ and $\mathit{ncol\_k}$ represent the structural dimensions extracted from `r_kampala_square`.

-   Each element $\beta^*_i$ from the `beta_smooth` vector is wrapped into the spatial grid following the row-major ordering system utilized by the `terra` environment.

**Methodological Implications**

-   **Geographic Alignment:** By cloning `r_kampala_square`, the newly generated `r_smooth` automatically inherits the original Coordinate Reference System (CRS) and geographic extent. This guarantees that the smoothed map will overlap with other vector layers of Kampala (such as `kampala_border`).

-   **Downstream Analysis:** The object `r_smooth` is now a fully functional spatial raster. It can be exported to a standard GeoTIFF file via `terra::writeRaster(r_smooth, "kampala_smoothed.tif")` or integrated into further spatial regressions.

```{r}
# 1. Clone the spatial structure of the square Kampala raster
r_smooth <- r_kampala_square

# 2. Automated Integrity Check
# Verify that the vector length matches the total number of raster cells (45 * 38 = 1710)
# This explicitly prevents any geometric distortion or spatial pixel shifting
stopifnot(length(beta_smooth) == terra::ncell(r_smooth))

# 3. Assign the estimated smoothed coefficients to the new raster object
# Since dimensions match perfectly, values are mapped sequentially without distortion
terra::values(r_smooth) <- beta_smooth

# 4. Print the spatial summary to verify data alignment
print(r_smooth)
```

This indicates that the fused lasso solution at $\lambda = 0.186$ retains a fine-grained spatial partition of the raster rather than aggregating pixels into a small number of large blocks.

# 2D Fused Lasso Model Fitting across Raster Time Series

## 1. Workspace Setup and File Selection

```{r}
# Define the files to process at the very beginning
# Change this index range here to update all loops automatically
files_to_process <- processed_files
```

```{r}
# Define and create the model-specific subfolder within the main fits directory
fused_lasso_fits_folder <- file.path(model_output_folder, "FusedLasso2D")

if (!dir.exists(fused_lasso_fits_folder)) {
  dir.create(fused_lasso_fits_folder)
}
```

## 2. 2D Fused Lasso Model Fitting

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Initialize the progress bar with elapsed time, ETA, and the active file token
pb <- progress_bar$new(
  format = " Processing [:bar] :percent | ETA: :eta | Elapsed: :elapsed | Active: :current_file",
  total = length(files_to_process),
  clear = FALSE,
  width = 95
)

for (f in files_to_process) {
  
  # Extract the clean file name without the extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  
  # Update the bar display 
  pb$tick(0, tokens = list(current_file = base_name))
  
  # Load the raster file
  r_kampala_square <- rast(f)
  
  # Extract pixel values as a continuous numeric vector
  v_kla_clean <- as.numeric(terra::values(r_kampala_square))
  
  # Store the spatial grid dimensions
  nrow_k <- terra::nrow(r_kampala_square)
  ncol_k <- terra::ncol(r_kampala_square)
  
  # Fit the 2D Fused Lasso model
  # dim1 maps to columns and dim2 maps to rows 
  # because terra extracts values row-by-row (Row-Major order)
  fit <- fusedlasso2d(
    y    = v_kla_clean,
    dim1 = ncol_k,
    dim2 = nrow_k
  )
  
  # Define the absolute target destination path using the directory variable
  output_path <- file.path(fused_lasso_fits_folder, paste0("fit_", base_name, ".rds"))
  
  # Serialize and save the model object directly to the disk drive
  saveRDS(fit, file = output_path)
  
  # Advance the progress percentage and update the tokens for the next round
  pb$tick(tokens = list(current_file = base_name))
}
```

```{r}
# Gather all serialized RDS model file paths from the target directory
saved_files <- list.files(fused_lasso_fits_folder, pattern = "\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)

for (f in saved_files) {
  
  # Extract the original variable name from the file metadata string
  var_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  
  # De-serialize the object and reconstruct it back into the global environment
  assign(var_name, readRDS(f), envir = .GlobalEnv)
}
```

## 3. Optimal Regularization Selection via Spatial Lag-K BIC

```{r}
# Initialize a list to store the BIC results for each file
bic_results <- list()

for (f in files_to_process) {
  
  # Extract the clean file name without the extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  
  # Retrieve the previously saved fit object from the global environment
  fit_name <- paste0("fit_", base_name)
  fit <- get(fit_name, envir = .GlobalEnv)
  
  # Load the raster file and extract grid properties
  r_kampala_square <- rast(f)
  v_kla_clean <- as.numeric(terra::values(r_kampala_square))
  nrow_k <- terra::nrow(r_kampala_square)
  ncol_k <- terra::ncol(r_kampala_square)
  
  # Extract the original data matrix from the raster object
  mat <- terra::as.matrix(r_kampala_square, wide = TRUE)
  
  # Configure Autocorrelation Function (ACF) parameters
  max_lag <- 10
  acf_rows <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(mat), ncol = max_lag + 1)
  
  # Compute row-by-row ACF to isolate local pixel behavior
  for(i in 1:nrow(mat)) {
    acf_rows[i, ] <- acf(mat[i, ], lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)$acf
  }
  acf_mean_horizontal <- colMeans(acf_rows)
  
  # Define the critical threshold for local decorrelation
  decorrelation_threshold <- 0.20
  
  # Extract the optimal lag dropping below the threshold (excluding lag 0)
  optimal_step <- which(acf_mean_horizontal[-1] < decorrelation_threshold)[1]
  
  # Automatic fallback if no lag drops below the specified threshold
  if (is.na(optimal_step)) optimal_step <- 3
  
  # Data Preparation for BIC evaluation
  y_vec <- as.numeric(v_kla_clean)
  n <- length(y_vec)
  beta_mat <- as.matrix(fit$beta) 
  
  # Calculate Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)
  rss <- colSums((beta_mat - y_vec)^2)
  df_vec <- fit$df
  
  # Reshape Original Data Vector to 2D Spatial Grid
  mat_grid <- matrix(y_vec, nrow = nrow_k, ncol = ncol_k, byrow = TRUE)
  
  # Estimate Error Variance (Sigma^2) via Spatial Lag-K Neumann Estimator
  diff_h <- mat_grid[, -(1:optimal_step), drop = FALSE] - mat_grid[, -((ncol(mat_grid) - (optimal_step - 1)):ncol(mat_grid)), drop = FALSE]
  diff_v <- mat_grid[-(1:optimal_step), , drop = FALSE] - mat_grid[-((nrow(mat_grid) - (optimal_step - 1)):nrow(mat_grid)), , drop = FALSE]
  
  # Final Lag-K Neumann variance estimate
  sig2_est <- (mean(diff_h^2) + mean(diff_v^2)) / 4
  
  # Compute Sparsity-Stable BIC Score vector
  bic_values_psbic <- (rss / sig2_est) + (df_vec * log(n))
  
  # Save the complete vector of BIC values into the storage list
  bic_results[[base_name]] <- bic_values_psbic
}
```

## 4. 5. Smoothed Raster Generation and Geometrical Integrity Check

```{r}
# Initialize a list to store the final smoothed coefficients for each file
smoothed_results <- list()

for (f in files_to_process) {
  
  # Extract the clean file name without the extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  
  # Retrieve the previously saved fit object from the global environment
  fit_name <- paste0("fit_", base_name)
  fit <- get(fit_name, envir = .GlobalEnv)
  
  # Retrieve the calculated BIC vector for this file
  current_bic <- bic_results[[base_name]]
  
  # Identify the index of the lowest BIC value
  best_idx <- which.min(current_bic)
  
  # Extract the optimal lambda value from the model path
  selected_lambda <- fit$lambda[best_idx]
  
  # Extract the smoothed beta coefficients for the selected optimal lambda
  beta_smooth <- coef(fit, lambda = selected_lambda)$beta
  
  # Save the smoothed vector into the storage list
  smoothed_results[[base_name]] <- beta_smooth
}
```

```{r}
# Initialize a list to store the final smoothed raster layers
smoothed_rasters <- list()

for (f in files_to_process) {
  
  # Extract the clean file name without the extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  
  # Load the original raster file to clone its spatial structure
  r_kampala_square <- rast(f)
  r_smooth <- r_kampala_square
  
  # Retrieve the calculated smoothed coefficients for this file
  beta_smooth <- smoothed_results[[base_name]]
  
  # Automated Integrity Check
  # Verify that the vector length matches the total number of raster cells
  stopifnot(length(beta_smooth) == terra::ncell(r_smooth))
  
  # Assign the estimated smoothed coefficients to the new raster object
  terra::values(r_smooth) <- beta_smooth
  
  # Save the final raster object into the storage list
  smoothed_rasters[[base_name]] <- r_smooth
}
```

## 6. Spatial Comparative Visualization: Original vs. Fused Lasso Data

```{r}
# Define and create the model-specific subfolder within the main plots directory
fused_lasso_plots_folder <- file.path(plots_output_folder, "FusedLasso2D")

if (!dir.exists(fused_lasso_plots_folder)) {
  dir.create(fused_lasso_plots_folder)
}
```

```{r}
for (f in files_to_process) {
  
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(f))
  
  # Load original raster and compute scale limits
  r_original <- rast(f)
  v_kla_clean <- as.numeric(terra::values(r_original))
  min_val <- min(v_kla_clean, na.rm = TRUE)
  max_val <- max(v_kla_clean, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Retrieve corresponding smoothed raster
  r_smooth <- smoothed_rasters[[base_name]]
  
  # Retrieve fit object and optimal lambda via BIC
  fit_name <- paste0("fit_", base_name)
  fit <- get(fit_name, envir = .GlobalEnv)
  current_bic <- bic_results[[base_name]]
  selected_lambda <- fit$lambda[which.min(current_bic)]
  
  bbox <- sf::st_bbox(r_original)
  x_range <- bbox["xmax"] - bbox["xmin"]
  y_range <- bbox["ymax"] - bbox["ymin"]
  pad_x <- x_range * 0.02   # 2% padding
  pad_y <- y_range * 0.02
  
  base_style <- list(
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "viridis",
      na.value = "transparent",
      name = "log(NTL)",
      limits = c(min_val, max_val),
      breaks = seq(0, max_val, by = 0.5)
    ),
    coord_sf(
      xlim = c(bbox["xmin"] - pad_x, bbox["xmax"] + pad_x),
      ylim = c(bbox["ymin"] - pad_y, bbox["ymax"] + pad_y),
      expand = FALSE
    ),
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 4)),
    theme_minimal(), 
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 12), 
      axis.text.y = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 0.5),
      legend.position = "right", 
      legend.key.height = unit(2, "cm"),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
    )
  )
  
  # 1. Generate original raster plot
  parts <- strsplit(base_name, "_")[[1]]
  year   <- parts[2]
  quarter <- parts[3]
  city   <- tools::toTitleCase(parts[4])  # "kampala" -> "Kampala"
  
  p1 <- ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r_original) +
    geom_sf(data = kampala_border, fill = NA, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.6) +
    labs(title = paste0(city, " (", quarter, " ", year, ") — Original")) +
    base_style
  
  # 2. Generate smoothed raster plot 
  p2 <- ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r_smooth) +
    labs(title = bquote(bold("Fused Lasso (" * lambda * " = " * .(round(selected_lambda, 3)) * ")"))) +
    base_style
  
  shared_legend <- cowplot::get_legend(p1)
  
  p1 <- p1 + theme(legend.position = "none")
  p2 <- p2 + theme(legend.position = "none")
  
  plots_combined <- cowplot::plot_grid(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
  
  final_grid <- cowplot::plot_grid(
    plots_combined, 
    shared_legend, 
    ncol = 2, 
    rel_widths = c(0.90, 0.10)
  )
  
  # Define the absolute target destination path for the output image file
  plot_output_path <- file.path(fused_lasso_plots_folder, paste0("FusedLasso2D_", base_name, ".png"))
  
  # Export and save the combined grid layout directly to the local storage drive
  ggsave(
    filename = plot_output_path,
    plot = final_grid,
    width = 12,
    height = 6,
    dpi = 300,
    bg = "white"
  )
  
  print(final_grid)
}
```
